transcript: Well, a month ago and six weeks ago, I said that I expected we would have a farm bill done and on the president's desk expecting a signature sometime around mid September. I am not that optimistic. The conferees met last week and it was just a pro forma setting was all that around the horn they spent a minute or two each saying what they wanted or didn't want. That is the biggest sticking point for a farm bill, and then should we get that resolved, then there's another big point that I think is very important to discuss, and it has real long-term implications all across this country. And that's going to be, you're expected already, Jeff, the King Amendment. or the Protect Interstate Commerce Act, which I introduced into the House version of the bill successfully in committee that passed the floor of the House for the second time in a row. And it is that we have states like California that are regulating the means and methods of production of agriculture products in other states. And so where I am right now, as we speak, I'm up in egg country. And we are, this is the number one egg producing congressional districts in America. And we have California has passed a regulation that required, first it was their producers had to double the cage size that the industry had for their laying ends. And then they realized they couldn't compete with the rest of the country. And so California passed a regulation that required any eggs being sold in California. to be certified to come from Ns that were in cages twice the industry standard size. So now we have Californian inspectors traveling into and around Iowa with their tape measures on their belt, going into our laying houses and measuring the cages and counting the Ns in each cage and deciding whether those eggs are suitable for Californians to eat. That's just one piece of this. It's also these circumstances are similar for banning gestation crates for sows for banning installs for veal cash, for denying the feeding of ducks and geese for forage or a liver. That's some of it. But the real thing is that our founding fathers established an enumerated power for Congress to regulate interstate commerce. Nobody else in the United States Congress because they wanted the states to be free trade salts. They didn't want to see that trade wars between the states. But California has already started the trade war by locking products out and specifying how they're produced. And so my legislation says this, that it bans the state from specifying and regulating the methods or means of production of agriculture products in other states. They can regulate their own producers, but they can't tell IOMs or Indians or anybody else how they're going to treat their livestock. And so that legislation needs to stay in that farm bill, if not. We're going to see all kinds of trade wars erupt between the state as the states regulate the means and methods of production of products in other states.

transcript: Well, Jeff, I don't know what the compromise would be. I'm making this argument with our leadership and with some of our administration. They'll say, We can't get this resolved because we can't get the stakeholders to sign off. Go right back at them and say, why would you think the stakeholders would sign off? If they could agree, they already would have done that and we wouldn't have this conversation. Petroleum has a significant advantage. They control the retail outlets and they've had their tax advantage for a lot of years. I'm not objecting to that. I'm saying give renewable fuels, give ethanol, biodiesel, market access. And whatever we might do to get petroleum industry to sign off, it's going to be something that is to the disadvantage, not the advantage of ethanol. And that's what I have said that clearly to Sonny Perdue, and I've said that clearly to Administrator Wheeler, I met with Administrator Wheeler the night he was in Iowa in his hotel for 40 minutes. We sat down, had a good and healthy conversation, I'd I, but I got nothing out of that conversation that gave me a lot of optimism walking out of there. He knew the issues, but he was looking still for the stakeholders to sign off. And in discussions with Secretary Perdue, just as recently as a day and a half ago, I pointed out to him that the best thing we can do for the markets is not $12 billion worth of bridge bailouts, just to bridge the whole. But the best thing we can do is let's go through, not just to, but through the E15. I don't want to see another blend wall like we had it while still having E10. I want that out of the way and let the market determine. And they have the power to do it. Administrator Wheeler, when I made the point to him about the RFS language that says, shall contain 10% ethanol. That specific language, I said to him, who wrote that language, and he got a kind of a funny look on his face, and he said, well, I did. And then I said, well, what was your intent? Was your intent to say, shall contain no more than 10%, or was it contained no less than 10%, and he said, well, I wish I'd been more specific. And then I said, but you can't tell me the intent. And he said, no. And I think he thought that was a good place for our conversation to be, but I responded, I said, good. I'm glad because If you can't tell us the intent, then no one can make the argument as to intent trumping the actual specific language. The language says shall contain 10%. That means it can have 10.1. It can have E20, 30, 50, E85. It all complies with the language you wrote, but if it's 9.9%, it does not because you can't argue that's 10%. So now we go back to the specific language and interpret the language. And you have all the legal authority you need to fix this and open the door up. And of course, we don't have that done yet.
